DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: MMR genes, especially mutS, are interstrain mosaics with high intragenic recombination and sequence patchwork, and repair efficiency for certain mismatches scales with local GC context. Mosaic variation in MutS’s mismatch-binding domains should shift recognition propensities for specific mismatch types and sequence environments, creating lineage-specific recombination windows across defined divergence spectra.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR).hypothesis: In regions harboring closely spaced sequence divergences, simultaneous MMR-directed excision from opposite strands generates double-strand breaks that are repaired by RecA-dependent gene conversion, contributing to genome-wide strand compositional biases linked to replication asymmetry.
DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: MMR operating on unmethylated DNA can produce DSBs via overlapping excision tracts, and such breaks are repaired by recombination; bacterial genomes show strand compositional biases correlating with replication direction. Therefore, MMR-mediated DSB formation at clusters of mismatches during recombination or replication across asymmetric strands can drive biased repair outcomes and enduring strand-skew patterns.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR).hypothesis: Targeted nickase-guided recombineering can flip MMR from an antirecombination to a pro-assimilation mode: placing a single-strand nick on the recipient strand adjacent to divergence directs strand-specific MMR excision and gap-filling to copy donor sequence across mismatches.
DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: Strand discrimination for MMR can be provided by nicks, which serve as entry points for excision; LPMR needs nicks or unmethylated GATC to act and normally aborts heteroduplexes between nonidentical sequences. Introducing a programmable nick on the recipient strand biases MMR to remove the recipient segment containing mismatches and resynthesize using the donor as template, converting the MMR barrier into a directional gene conversion mechanism across divergent DNA.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR).hypothesis: Dcm-dependent very-short-patch repair (VSP) functions as an epigenetic compatibility filter during horizontal transfer, preferentially correcting G·T mismatches arising from 5-methylcytosine deamination in a donor- and site-specific manner, thereby biasing fixation of incoming DNA based on cytosine methylation patterns.
DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: Repair of G·T mismatches at deaminated 5-meC sites requires E. coli cytosine methylase (Dcm) and MutS/MutL but not MutH, indicating a methylation-cued repair pathway distinct from canonical GATC-directed MMR. During HGT between taxa with differing Dcm patterns, VSP repair will asymmetrically correct G·T mismatches, filtering which donor sequences are retained, creating an epigenetically encoded barrier to gene flow.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR).hypothesis: Introducing sparse, strategically placed synonymous base substitutions (“microdivergence patches”) within one copy of human segmental duplications that mediate recurrent non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) will recruit MutS/MutL anti-recombination to heteroduplex intermediates and abort strand exchange, thereby reducing pathogenic CNV formation without disrupting gene function.
DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: MMR recognizes single-base mismatches in heteroduplex DNA and aborts recombination more effectively for base substitutions than for large heterologies, powerfully limiting recombination between diverged repeats. Seeding a minimal density of mismatches within repeat pairs should trigger MutS/L recognition during nascent strand exchange and prevent NAHR-driven rearrangements.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR).hypothesis: Targeted stabilization of duplex DNA at microsatellite tracts—by local GC-enrichment, minor-groove binding proteins, or dCas-based DNA-stiffening tethers—will enhance MMR recognition and correction of slippage intermediates in vivo, reducing pathogenic repeat expansions (e.g., Huntington’s, myotonic dystrophy).
DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: MMR operates most efficiently in regions of stable double helix, and increasing local G:C content near mismatches improves repair extent. Increasing local duplex stability at repeats should bias repair pathways toward efficient MMR-coupled correction of slipped-strand intermediates, decreasing expansion rates.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR).hypothesis: Overexpression of mismatch-binding proteins (MutS/MutL or their eukaryotic homologs) can be used as an engineered, tunable genetic firewall in production microbes to sharply reduce interspecies horizontal gene transfer and homeologous recombination without elevating mutation rate, enhancing biocontainment.
DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: Increasing MutS/L levels strengthens the anti-recombination barrier to sequence divergence while not lowering mutation rates under normal conditions. Thus, elevating MMR surveillance specifically raises the MEPS requirement for successful recombination, blocking acquisition of foreign DNA without fitness costs from hypermutability.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR).hypothesis: Tethering MMR components (e.g., MSH2–MSH6 and MLH1–PMS2 domains) to Cas9 nickases or base editors at edit sites will harness mismatch-provoked localized DNA synthesis to extend homology-directed gene conversion tracts (hundreds of bp to ~1 kb) without creating long resected DSBs, increasing precise editing efficiency and tract length.
DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: Mismatches provoke localized DNA synthesis that can extend up to kilobases and often begins at a distance from the mismatch. Localizing MMR sensors at programmed mismatches created by base editors or nick-induced heteroduplexes should recruit repair synthesis and polymerase tracts, enlarging conversion tracts while maintaining edit specificity.

DNA mismatch repair (MMR).hypothesis: Pharmacologic inhibition of σS or Hfq during antibiotic treatment will prevent stress-induced downregulation of MutS/MutH, maintain MMR activity, and thereby suppress MMR-dependent adaptive mutagenesis (MAC) and the emergence of antibiotic resistance in starving or stationary-phase bacterial populations.
DNA mismatch repair (MMR).rationale: MutS and MutH are downregulated via σS and Hfq in stationary phase, and MAC requires the methyl-directed mismatch repair system along with RecA and PolB. Blocking the σS/Hfq pathway should keep MMR functional under stress, reducing the mutation supply that fuels rapid resistance evolution.

Retropseudogene.hypothesis: Retroposition captures sequence-context-dependent transcriptional 'molecular misreading' events (e.g., GA dinucleotide deletions) into processed pseudogenes, creating a characteristic −GA frameshift signature at GA repeats that reveals the fidelity state of the source cell and the activity of tRNA modification pathways at the time of retrocopying.
Retropseudogene.rationale: GA-repeat regions undergo molecular misreading that deletes GA dinucleotides in the mRNA. If such error-bearing mRNAs are reverse transcribed during LINE-1-mediated retroposition, the resulting retropseudogenes will inherit these deletions, yielding a distinctive mutational spectrum that can be used to infer the cellular context of their formation.

Retropseudogene.hypothesis: Processed pseudogene fragments embedded within introns of gene families act as anti-recombination decoys by engaging MSH2/MSH6-based mismatch surveillance at short homeologous tracts, aborting strand exchange and thereby suppressing non-allelic homologous recombination; engineered retropseudogene shards could be deployed proximal to NAHR hotspots to stabilize vulnerable loci.
Retropseudogene.rationale: MutS-family proteins specifically interfere with homeologous strand exchange. Dispersed intronic, intronless retropseudogene fragments share limited homology with cognate genes, which is sufficient to trigger mismatch surveillance but below efficient recombination thresholds, thus biasing repair toward anti-recombination rather than productive exchange.

Retropseudogene.hypothesis: Stalling/idling of LINE-1 reverse transcriptase on structured or damaged RNA (e.g., oxidized bases) promotes template switching among co-expressed paralogous transcripts, generating chimeric 'patchwork' processed pseudogenes that mosaicize exons from multiple sources and seed exon-shuffling innovation.
Retropseudogene.rationale: Polymerase idling at impediments is known to cause repeated nucleotide turnover and stalls, conditions that favor template switching in other systems. Analogous stalling during retrocopy synthesis would mechanistically enable RT to hop between similar RNA templates, yielding chimeric retropseudogenes with mosaic sequence tracts.

Retropseudogene.hypothesis: Transient attenuation of MSH2-dependent anti-homeologous recombination in germinal center B cells permits dispersed processed pseudogenes to serve as gene-conversion donors for immunoglobulin V regions outside canonical donor arrays, expanding repertoire diversity while increasing off-target risk.
Retropseudogene.rationale: Somatic diversification by gene conversion can use silent pseudogenes as sequence donors. Because MutS-family activity suppresses homeologous exchange, temporarily reducing MSH2 function should allow broader donor usage, including dispersed retropseudogenes sharing patchy homology with V segments.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Oxidative post-translational modification of the 3′→5′ exonuclease (proofreading) subunit of the replicative DNA polymerase acts as a stress-controlled mutator switch in bacteria, transiently reducing proofreading during SOS and thereby fixing mutations on undamaged DNA.
Mutagenicity.rationale: Evidence suggests induced mutagenesis depends on regulation of 3′→5′ exonuclease activity, and protein damage can be more mutagenic than DNA damage. We hypothesize that oxidative modifications (e.g., cysteine sulfenylation/carbonylation) of the epsilon (DnaQ) subunit or its interaction with the β-clamp lower proofreading fidelity during SOS, elevating genome-wide mutation fixation even without lesions.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: ROSE mutagenesis in resting Escherichia coli is driven by nucleotide excision repair (NER)-initiated gap filling by DNA polymerase I that misincorporates oxidized dNTPs (notably 8-oxo-dGTP), and is specifically suppressible by boosting MutT activity.
Mutagenicity.rationale: ROSE mutagenesis requires uvrB (NER) and polA (Pol I), pointing to repair-patch synthesis as the source of mutations in non-replicating cells. Because 8-oxo-dGTP is a potent misincorporated mutagenic substrate and MutT sanitizes it, we predict that oxidized nucleotide pools fuel ROSE mutagenesis via Pol I during NER patching.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: In non-dividing mammalian cells, NER-initiated gap filling by DNA polymerase β is a dominant source of spontaneous mutagenesis through incorporation of oxidized dNTPs, and mammalian MutT homologs (e.g., MTH1/NUDT1) act as antimutators in this repair-context; upregulating MTH1 will reduce mutation accumulation in aging post-mitotic tissues.
Mutagenicity.rationale: Resting-cell mutagenesis in bacteria provides a paradigm for non-replicating eukaryotic cells. Given the presence of MutT homologs in mammals, we propose that oxidized dNTP sanitization modulates error-prone repair synthesis during NER in neurons and other post-mitotic cells.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: The bacterial SOS network directly downregulates mismatch repair by LexA-dependent repression of mutS/mutL transcription, jointly elevating point mutation rates and permitting recombination between diverged sequences during stress.
Mutagenicity.rationale: Stress upregulates SOS mutagenesis while mismatch repair (MRS) activity declines, both increasing genetic variability. We hypothesize a direct regulatory link: LexA binding sites in mutS/mutL promoters reduce MMR during SOS, mechanistically coupling stress sensing to both mutation and anti-recombination relief.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Proteome carbonylation selectively impairs mismatch repair (MutS/MutL) and replicative proofreading, generating cell-to-cell mutation rate heterogeneity proportional to protein oxidation levels; antioxidant interventions that lower protein carbonylation will reduce spontaneous and induced mutagenesis without altering DNA lesion burden.
Mutagenicity.rationale: A gradient of protein carbonylation correlates with variation in induced mutagenesis and spontaneous mutation rates, and protein damage can be more mutagenic than DNA damage. We propose that oxidation of MMR and proofreading components underlies this link, making proteome protection an antimutator strategy.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: During SOS, processed UmuD′ engages the β-clamp to allosterically displace or inhibit the ε (DnaQ) proofreading subunit, switching the replisome into a low-specificity ‘mutator mode’ that generates mutations on undamaged DNA genome-wide.
Mutagenicity.rationale: Inducible mutator activity in SOS causes mutagenesis of undamaged DNA, and control of proofreading is implicated in induced mutation rates. We posit a concrete interaction in the replisome: UmuD′-β-clamp complexes transiently reduce exonuclease access, increasing error retention beyond lesion sites.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: MutL foci dynamics in live bacteria report replication-independent mismatches arising during repair synthesis under oxidative stress; small molecules that stabilize MutL–mismatch complexes will bias processing toward correction over fixation, lowering the rate of emergence of antibiotic resistance.
Mutagenicity.rationale: MutL foci mark nascent mutations in vivo. We hypothesize that, under oxidative stress, a significant fraction of these foci originate from repair-associated mismatches, and that pharmacologically modulating MutL-DNA interaction kinetics can shift the outcome toward repair rather than mutation fixation.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Transient 2–4-fold attenuation of MutLα activity during CRISPR-mediated homology-directed repair will relax MMR-imposed homeology rejection and enable efficient knock-in with polymorphic donor DNA without inducing a mutator phenotype, because MutL specifically sets homology discrimination in recombination independently of replication error repair.
Mutagenicity.rationale: A hypomorphic MutL state produces hyperrecombination without increased point mutagenesis, indicating a separable recombination-control function. Since MMR suppresses non-isogenic gene replacement, temporally tuning MutL should widen the effective homology window while preserving replication fidelity.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Oxidative carbonylation of the β-clamp/PCNA enhances binding and retention of mutagenic translesion polymerases, thereby amplifying damage-induced mutagenesis under oxidative stress; thiol antioxidants should suppress mutagenesis by protecting clamp proteins even without reducing ROS levels.
Mutagenicity.rationale: Mutagenesis by E. coli Pol IV requires its interaction with the β-clamp, and protein oxidation can be a dominant driver of mutagenic outcomes. Carbonylation of clamp surfaces is predicted to alter partner exchange kinetics toward TLS polymerases, increasing error-prone synthesis.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: UV-induced carbonylation of specific KRAS residues at or near the RAF1-binding interface transiently diminishes RAF1 activation and rewires MAPK signaling, creating selective pressure for compensatory DNA mutations in RAS pathway genes during early photocarcinogenesis.
Mutagenicity.rationale: Mass spectrometry identifies UV-driven KRAS carbonylations, and mutations at the KRAS–RAF1 interface reduce RAF1 activation; analogous oxidative adducts should similarly impede binding, modulating survival signaling and shaping which genomic mutations are subsequently fixed.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Elevating cellular MutL abundance prevents MMR saturation under high mismatch load and suppresses adaptive mutagenesis and homeologous recombination during stress, thereby reducing the emergence of antibiotic resistance with minimal fitness cost.
Mutagenicity.rationale: When mismatch burden is high, MMR saturation is caused by MutL limitation; MutL foci track mutation frequency. Increasing MutL should maintain mismatch processing capacity and preserve recombination gating even under stress.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Strategically methylating donor DNA at GATC sites will bias MutH-directed strand incision to the chromosomal strand during MMR, favoring incorporation of polymorphic donor sequences and overcoming MMR suppression of homeologous recombination in bacterial gene replacement.
Mutagenicity.rationale: Dam methylation provides MMR strand discrimination, and MMR reduces recombination when sequences are nonidentical; imposing methylation asymmetry should coerce MMR to excise the genomic strand mismatches rather than reject the donor.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Engineering a MutL variant that recognizes Red-mediated single-strand annealing intermediates will restore MMR-dependent homeology discrimination to phage-derived recombineering systems, thereby blocking horizontal transfer of divergent DNA across species barriers.
Mutagenicity.rationale: MutS is ineffective on Red-mediated recombination, indicating an MMR blind spot, while MutL defines effective homology in recombination control; retargeting MutL to Red-specific intermediates should impose a homology checkpoint on this pathway.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Small-molecule disruption of the σS/Hfq-mediated downregulation of MutS in stationary-phase bacteria will prevent stress-induced adaptive mutagenesis by maintaining mismatch repair activity under carbon starvation and oxidative respiration, thereby suppressing the emergence of antibiotic resistance during therapy.
Mutagenicity.rationale: MutS (and mutH) levels drop to undetectable in starving cells via σS- and Hfq-dependent control, rendering MMR practically non-functional in stationary phase, a setting where stress-induced mutagenesis operates. Pharmacologically blocking the σS/Hfq control of mutS should keep MMR active and blunt MAC-driven adaptive mutation during treatment.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: CRISPR/dCas9-tethered, locus-specific sequestration of MutS/MutL will transiently relax the MMR barrier to homeologous recombination only at the targeted site, enabling precise gene replacement across 1–5% sequence divergence in mammalian cells without global mutagenesis.
Mutagenicity.rationale: MMR blocks recombination between non-isogenic donor DNA and the host genome, and this barrier vanishes in MSH2−/− ES cells. Local, temporary inhibition of MMR at the edit locus should recapitulate the MMR-deficient recombination permissiveness without genome-wide hypermutation.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Phage-delivered overexpression of MutS/MutL in pathogenic bacteria will selectively reduce horizontal gene transfer by raising the MMR-mediated barrier to homeologous recombination, limiting acquisition of resistance and virulence islands while leaving baseline point mutation rates largely unchanged.
Mutagenicity.rationale: Overproduction of mismatch-binding proteins increases the recombination barrier with sequence divergence (steeper slope), curbing gene exchange, and does not appreciably lower mutation rates, minimizing fitness costs of the intervention. Phage vectors can deliver this transiently during infection.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: In vivo, MutL polymerization at mismatches is nucleated and stabilized by transcription-derived R-loops, forming a proteinaceous barrier that halts RecA-catalyzed branch migration across mismatches; in vitro systems lacking R-loops default to a DNA-looping mechanism, explaining the in vitro/in vivo discrepancy.
Mutagenicity.rationale: The observed inconsistency between DNA-loop models in vitro and MutL aggregation/polymerization in vivo suggests a missing cofactor in vitro. R-loops provide persistent RNA–DNA hybrids at transcribed regions that could scaffold MutL accumulation and alter branch migration dynamics around mismatches.

Mutagenicity.hypothesis: Nonmutagenic tumor promoters such as TPA drive carcinogenesis by inducing mitotic recombination and sister chromatid exchanges that cause loss of heterozygosity at tumor suppressor loci; selective inhibition of promoter-induced SCE signaling will reduce promotion-driven tumor formation.
Mutagenicity.rationale: TPA uniquely elevates SCEs without detectable DNA damage, mutagenesis, or toxicity, consistent with a promotion mechanism via recombination-mediated LOH rather than new point mutations. Targeting the signaling that links promoter action to SCEs should blunt this LOH-based promotion.

Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.hypothesis: Oxidative protein carbonylation of genome stability factors (e.g., cohesin/condensin subunits, BLM/RECQ helicases) functions as a mechanistic tumor promoter by shifting DNA damage processing toward mitotic recombination, thereby accelerating loss of heterozygosity at pre-initiated tumor suppressor loci; carbonyl-scavenging or proteostasis-enhancing interventions will suppress promotion by specifically reducing SCE/mitotic recombination without altering point-mutation frequency.
Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.rationale: Protein carbonylation rises with oxidative stress and correlates with sharply increased spontaneous mutagenesis; tumor promoters correlate with SCE/recombinational activity that drives LOH. If carbonylation disables high-fidelity repair and biases toward recombination, then reducing carbonylation should blunt promotion by preventing LOH in initiated cells.

Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.hypothesis: Tumor promoters activate an extracellular protease cascade (e.g., plasminogen activator) that transiently inactivates mismatch repair and anti-recombination factors via proteolysis, inducing a reversible 'mutator–recombinator' state that drives fixation of initiation events through LOH; specific trypsin-like protease inhibitors (e.g., antipain, leupeptin) prevent this by preserving MMR/anti-recombination integrity.
Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.rationale: Promoters induce protease activity, and protease inhibitors suppress both UV mutagenesis and promotion-linked outcomes. A protease-driven degradation of MMR/anti-recombination proteins would mechanistically explain increased SCE/LOH during promotion and the protective effect of antiproteases.

Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.hypothesis: Site-specific carbonylation of KRAS under oxidative/UV stress enhances RAF recruitment and MEK–ERK pathway activation independent of KRAS mutation by stabilizing the RAF–RAS complex and/or reducing intrinsic GTPase activity; pharmacologic carbonyl-scavengers will diminish RAS pathway signaling in oxidative microenvironments and act as antitumor promoters.
Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.rationale: UV elevates KRAS carbonylation on defined residues, and KRAS–RAF engagement is the key activation step that is difficult to drug directly. If carbonylation alters KRAS conformational dynamics toward a RAF-favorable state, then preventing carbonyl adduct formation should dampen downstream signaling without directly targeting KRAS.

Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.hypothesis: Inflammation-driven nitric oxide and ROS maintain initiated, slow-cycling stem/progenitor cells in a quiescent but mutagenic state with time-dependent accumulation of replication-independent DNA lesions that are converted upon re-entry into S-phase into elevated SCE/LOH events; thus, promoters that enforce or prolong quiescence under oxidative load paradoxically accelerate the initiation-to-promotion transition.
Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.rationale: Resting eukaryotic cells can accrue mutations at a constant rate per time, and inflammatory cytokines generate NO/ROS. A mechanistic sequence where quiescent initiated cells accumulate lesions that are resolved via recombination upon cell-cycle re-entry explains promotion-associated SCE/LOH and predicts that modulating redox/quiescence alters promotion efficiency.

Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.hypothesis: Local sequence mismatches created by the first (initiating) mutation at a tumor suppressor gene establish a mismatch-stimulated anti-recombination barrier that normally suppresses LOH; tumor promoters overcome this by activating protease-driven signaling that downregulates anti-recombination machinery, transiently lifting the barrier and enabling centromere-proximal crossovers that convert m/+ to m/m.
Carcinogenesis (multistage, initiation–p.rationale: Mismatch-stimulated anti-recombination can block recombination between diverged sequences, and promotion is tied to recombinational events that produce homozygosity at recessive loci. A promoter-induced suppression of anti-recombination factors provides a mechanistic switch that allows LOH precisely where the first hit has created local heterology.

Hallmarks of aging.hypothesis: Age-associated oxidation of ribosomal A-site components (rRNA and proximal ribosomal proteins) increases +1 frameshifting and mistranslation, creating a feed-forward loop that amplifies proteome carbonylation and proteostasis collapse; mitochondria-permeant thiol-redox modulators that selectively stabilize ribosomal thiols will restore translational fidelity and slow cellular aging.
Hallmarks of aging.rationale: A-site vacancy correlates with +1 frameshifting, and antibiotic-induced misreading increases oxidized, aggregated proteins that accumulate with age. Aging is accompanied by thiol/disulfide disequilibrium, suggesting that oxidation of ribosomal components could mechanistically drive error-prone translation and proteome damage; stabilizing ribosome redox state should break this loop.

Hallmarks of aging.hypothesis: Site-specific carbonylation of KRAS in aging dermal fibroblasts biases RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK signaling toward MMP-1 induction and mitochondrial dysfunction, thereby driving extracellular matrix degradation and skin aging; preventing or enzymatically reversing KRAS carbonylation within RAS nanodomains will normalize MAPK signaling and mitigate dermal aging.
Hallmarks of aging.rationale: KRAS acquires defined carbonylation modifications under oxidative stress, and aged skin shows increased protein carbonylation with MMP-1 induction and reduced respiration. This suggests a mechanistic route wherein oxidative adducts on KRAS alter effector engagement and downstream outputs relevant to skin aging.

Hallmarks of aging.hypothesis: Active immunization against canonical protein carbonyl and AGE neoepitopes will enhance immunological ‘sanitation’ of senescent and damaged cells and matrix, reduce NF-κB–driven inflammaging, and delay multimorbidity in aging.
Hallmarks of aging.rationale: Immunity participates in the elimination of abnormal and senescent cells, while AGEs and carbonylated proteins accumulate with age and trigger inflammation. A vaccine that focuses immune clearance on these conserved damage-associated neoepitopes could mechanistically restore tissue clean-up capacity.

Hallmarks of aging.hypothesis: A mitochondria-targeted Deinococcus radiodurans–inspired Mn2+–small metabolite complex will preserve the cellular proteome during inflammatory or viral stress, maintaining oxidative phosphorylation, lowering lactate output, and alleviating long-COVID–like fatigue and age-related energy failure.
Hallmarks of aging.rationale: D. radiodurans radioprotection arises from Mn2+-rich metabolite cocktails that shield the proteome, and redox imbalance with mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated lactate characterizes severe and post-acute COVID-19. Delivering such complexes to mitochondria should directly protect respiratory chain proteins and normalize metabolism.

Hallmarks of aging.hypothesis: Transient mitochondrial ROS bursts oxidize guanosines in selected neuronal mRNAs (8-oxo-G), especially those encoding proteostasis factors, causing mistranslation and initiating a feed-forward proteome damage loop underlying selective neuronal vulnerability; engineered mRNA-binding antioxidants or proteins that shield guanosines will block this loop and delay neurodegeneration with aging.
Hallmarks of aging.rationale: 8-oxo-G accumulates in RNA of vulnerable neurons and correlates with altered protein synthesis. Coupled with proteostasis defects in neurodegeneration, targeted prevention of mRNA oxidation offers a mechanistic intervention point upstream of aggregate formation.

Proteostasis.hypothesis: Pharmacologically enhancing translational fidelity (e.g., via small-molecule activators of aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase editing or ribosomal proofreading) will lower the intracellular burden of aberrant proteins, thereby reducing protein carbonylation and suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation under stress in mammalian cells.
Proteostasis.rationale: Oxidative protein damage is limited by the level of aberrant proteins; decreasing misfolded/mistranslated protein production should proportionally reduce carbonylation and downstream redox-driven inflammation. Consequently, fewer oxidized protein danger signals will reduce NLRP3 activation and cytokine output.

Proteostasis.hypothesis: Engineering LEA-like, low-complexity hydrophilic peptides fused to mitochondrial targeting sequences will function as in situ antioxidant-chaperone ‘shells’ that suppress mitochondrial protein aggregation and carbonylation during acute oxidative stress, thereby preventing NLRP3 activation and cytokine storm.
Proteostasis.rationale: LEA proteins suppress aggregation and inactivation under water/oxidative stress; directing such LC-rich chaperone-like activity to mitochondria should preserve mitoproteostasis and blunt the redox signals that trigger inflammasome activation.

Proteostasis.hypothesis: Topical delivery of a Mn2+/orthophosphate/dipeptide ultrafiltrate designed to raise the local Mn/Fe ratio in dermis will protect the skin proteome from UV/oxidant-induced carbonylation, preserve proteasome activity with age, and suppress AP‑1/NF‑κB‑mediated MMP‑1 induction, delaying skin aging.
Proteostasis.rationale: High intracellular Mn/Fe ratios correlate with proteome protection, and Mn–Pi–amino acid complexes protect proteins from carbonylation; preserving proteostasis should prevent the proteasome decline linked to MMP‑1 upregulation in aging fibroblasts.

Proteostasis.hypothesis: Upregulating peptide and amino acid import (e.g., via pharmacologic activation of peptide transporters such as SLC15 family) in aging cells will accelerate proteome renewal and reverse p53/Rb‑dependent senescence induced by partial proteasome decline by supplying substrates for rapid replacement of damaged proteins.
Proteostasis.rationale: Radiation‑resistant bacteria deploy extensive peptide/AA import to fuel recovery and repair; similarly boosting nutrient influx in senescent mammalian cells should support proteome turnover and restore proteostasis despite reduced UPS capacity.

Proteostasis.hypothesis: Oxidation-induced disruption of the KRAS–RAF interface can be leveraged as a selective oncogenic checkpoint by creating PROTAC-like molecules or engineered E3 ligases that recognize carbonylated RAF and promote its ubiquitination and degradation, thereby dampening RAS–ERK signaling in RAS-driven cancers.
Proteostasis.rationale: Protein carbonylation disrupts KRAS/RAF binding; a degradation system that preferentially binds oxidized RAF would convert redox damage into a selective removal signal, reducing oncogenic flux while sparing non-oxidized proteins in normal contexts.

Proteostasis.hypothesis: Proteome-protective antioxidant systems that preserve protein conformation will reduce mismatch repair–dependent lethality during base analog (e.g., 2‑AP) exposure by preventing oxidative misregulation of MutS/MutH/UvrD, thereby lowering aberrant endonucleolytic activity and improving cell viability.
Proteostasis.rationale: Viability loss under 2‑AP requires MutS/MutH/UvrD; if proteome oxidation drives dysfunctional MMR execution, then stabilizing these proteins against oxidative damage should mitigate lethal cleavage and enhance survival during genotoxic stress.

Carcinogenicity.hypothesis: Tumor promoters elevate proteome carbonylation that biases DNA repair toward recombinogenic sister chromatid exchange, thereby amplifying loss-of-heterozygosity at pre-existing heterozygous tumor suppressor loci in initiated cells; antiproteases/anti-inflammatories inhibit promotion in part by lowering protein carbonylation and restoring high-fidelity repair.
Carcinogenicity.rationale: Promotion is linked to SCE-type recombinogenic activity, and cancers show increased protein carbonylation which causally elevates mutation burdens. A carbonylation-driven shift in repair pathway choice provides a mechanistic bridge from nonmutagenic promoters to LOH-driven malignant progression and explains why antiproteases suppress both SCE and tumorigenesis.

Carcinogenicity.hypothesis: A trypsin-like serine protease acts as a master switch for an inducible mammalian ‘SOS-like’ response by proteolytically inactivating a repressor of translesion synthesis and recombinogenic repair; inhibiting this protease suppresses both initiation mutagenesis and promotion-driven LOH without impairing high-fidelity repair.
Carcinogenicity.rationale: Protease inhibitors suppress UV mutagenesis in bacteria and inhibit tumor promotion in mice, while mutagenic pathways can be inducible. A conserved protease-gated regulatory node would unify these phenomena and yields a druggable target to blunt both initiating and promoting steps.

Carcinogenicity.hypothesis: Promotion-driven increases in recombination/SCE preferentially generate loss-of-heterozygosity at antigen presentation genes (e.g., B2M/HLA), enabling immune escape of initiated clones that would otherwise be eliminated by cytotoxic T cells, thereby constituting an immune-evasive mechanism of tumor promotion.
Carcinogenicity.rationale: Initiated cells expressing non-self proteins are killed by killer T cells, while promotion elevates recombinogenic activity. If promotion increases LOH at antigen presentation loci, clones lose MHC-I display and evade immune surveillance, accelerating malignant outgrowth.

Carcinogenicity.hypothesis: Protein carbonylation of cohesin/condensin and replication fork protection factors accelerates the rate-limiting chromosomal rearrangement step in carcinogenesis; antioxidant or carbonyl-scavenging interventions that preserve these complexes’ function will reduce malignant conversion even after initiation.
Carcinogenicity.rationale: Chromosomal rearrangement is a rate-limiting step in carcinogenesis, and proteome carbonylation causally elevates mutational stress and is abundant in cancer cells. Carbonyl damage to chromosomal architecture proteins provides a mechanistic route to rearrangements that can be therapeutically targeted.

Carcinogenicity.hypothesis: Carcinogenic potency of an exposure is determined by a nonlinear threshold behavior proportional to the product of its initiating mutagenic burden and its recombinogenic (promotion) activity; therefore, co-exposures to weak initiators and weak promoters can become highly carcinogenic when their product exceeds a critical threshold.
Carcinogenicity.rationale: Quantitative analyses indicate that the product of mutagenic and recombinogenic potencies best correlates with carcinogenic potency. A mechanistic product-rule predicts threshold effects and synergisms that can be tested by jointly modulating mutation load and SCE frequency.

Carcinogenicity.hypothesis: Therapeutic, temporally controlled activation of high-fidelity homologous recombination in early neoplasms can drive gene conversion that restores heterozygosity at tumor suppressor loci, exploiting the observed carcinogen-induced reversion phenomenon to reverse malignant traits without introducing new mutations.
Carcinogenicity.rationale: The same agents can induce both transformed clones and reversion to normal, implying that recombination dynamics can correct malignant genotypes. Biasing repair toward error-free HR in a defined window could mechanistically enable reversion of LOH at tumor suppressors.

Bacterial conjugation.hypothesis: Co-delivery of short, UV-damaged “decoy” DNA fragments during conjugation will transiently induce SOS in the recipient, suppressing restriction and RecBCD exonuclease V activity and thereby protecting co-transferred undamaged donor DNA to yield higher-frequency and longer RecBCD-mediated chromosomal replacements across interspecies sequence divergence.
Bacterial conjugation.rationale: UV-damaged donor DNA entering a nonirradiated recipient is sufficient to induce SOS. SOS induction alleviates restriction and inhibits ExoV, while RecBCD mediates large chromosomal replacements during interspecies conjugational recombination. Therefore, engineered decoy lesion fragments should gate the recipient into a pro-recombination state precisely when donor DNA arrives, increasing both recombination frequency and tract length.

Bacterial conjugation.hypothesis: A conjugative plasmid encoding an SOS-responsive CRISPRi or dominant-negative peptide module that transiently suppresses MutS/MutL during mating will enable efficient homeologous recombination of divergent DNA in the recipient while restoring MMR post-integration to minimize long-term mutational burden.
Bacterial conjugation.rationale: MMR is the principal barrier to interspecies recombination and its loss greatly enhances horizontal gene transfer, yet permanent MMR loss is deleterious. Because mating induces SOS in recipients, placing MMR-suppressing functions under SOS control should temporally disable MMR only during DNA entry and recombination, then re-enable it afterward.

Bacterial conjugation.hypothesis: Engineering donor homology arms with isolated, strategically placed mismatches flanked by correctly methylated GATC sites will bias mismatch repair toward localized gene conversion rather than heteroduplex rejection, overcoming the quantitative recombination barrier imposed by modest sequence divergence without disabling MMR.
Bacterial conjugation.rationale: Mismatch repair can execute localized gene conversion and requires GATC-directed strand discrimination, while small polymorphism levels already act as recombination barriers. By tuning mismatch placement and dam-methylation context, MMR can be converted from an anti-recombinational editor into a pro-recombinational converter at recombination intermediates.

Bacterial conjugation.hypothesis: The amplitude of SOS induction in recipients at the moment of mating quantitatively increases the length of RecBCD-mediated chromosomal replacements during interspecies conjugation by inhibiting ExoV and restriction, shifting RecBCD processing from degradation toward recombination.
Bacterial conjugation.rationale: Mating elicits a genuine SOS response; SOS suppresses restriction and ExoV. Because RecBCD is the major pathway for interspecies conjugational recombination and is responsible for large chromosomal replacements, higher SOS levels should prolong donor DNA survival and extend recombination tracts.

Bacterial conjugation.hypothesis: An SOS-responsive recA overexpression module in the recipient will produce a transient RecA pulse during conjugation that enhances strand exchange across mismatches, increasing interspecies recombination frequency without chronic RecA overproduction.
Bacterial conjugation.rationale: RecA is essential for interspecies recombination and constitutive RecA elevation stimulates both intra- and interspecies conjugational recombination. Using mating-induced SOS as a native trigger to transiently raise RecA should improve homeologous recombination efficiency while avoiding long-term perturbation.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: AT-selective minor-groove binders will bias replication-error correction toward DNA polymerase 3′→5′ proofreading by stabilizing extrahelical mispairs in AT-rich tracts, thereby enhancing exonuclease engagement at the nascent 3′ end and reducing mutational hotspots in contingency gene microsatellites.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Poorly repaired mismatches in AT-rich regions often adopt extrahelical configurations that are preferentially corrected by polymerase-associated proofreading, and T4 polymerase proofreading is most active in AT-rich contexts. Small AT-minor-groove ligands (e.g., distamycin-like) that subtly narrow the groove and promote local base flipping should increase the frequency of 3′-end fraying and mispair extrusion, kinetically favoring exonuclease editing over mismatch repair.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: A specific interaction surface between RecA* filaments and the ε (DnaQ) proofreading subunit of DNA polymerase III suppresses 3′→5′ exonuclease activity at stalled forks to license SOS polymerase access; disrupting this interface will maintain proofreading at damage-stalled termini and suppress SOS-dependent mutagenesis without blocking recombinational repair.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: RecA has been shown to inhibit the Pol III-associated proofreading exonuclease and to lower replicase fidelity, while RecA* is the platform for Pol V activity. This suggests a mechanistic gate in which RecA* directly impedes ε-mediated editing to promote TLS polymerase takeover; targeting that gate should restore proofreading and reduce mutagenesis.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Cellular SSB concentration dynamically partitions replication-error correction between proofreading and mismatch repair by suppressing extrahelical mispair formation; lowering local SSB availability near the fork will increase polymerase 3′→5′ exonuclease engagement in AT-rich regions, whereas elevated SSB will shunt errors to MMR.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: SSB is expected to prevent extrahelical base conformations that favor proofreading-based correction, while mismatches that persist in an extrahelical state are preferentially edited by the polymerase exonuclease. Thus, SSB levels should tune the structural state of mispairs and thereby the choice of correction pathway.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: PCNA post-translational modification state (e.g., monoubiquitination) allosterically regulates the proofreading–polymerization switch of replicative eukaryotic polymerases at nascent mismatches, such that unmodified PCNA promotes 3′→5′ exonuclease engagement while modified PCNA suppresses proofreading to facilitate lesion bypass and subsequent MMR.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: PCNA has repair-synthesis–independent roles in NER, implying clamp-mediated signaling functions beyond polymerase tethering. Extending this, PCNA modifications could alter polymerase conformational equilibria to favor or disfavor exonuclease engagement at mismatches, coordinating proofreading with downstream repair pathways.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: A synthetic DNA-binding adaptor that targets short microsatellite tracts and simultaneously engages the β-clamp will locally increase the dwell time of the replicative polymerase in the exonuclease state, thereby suppressing slippage and frameshift mutagenesis that escape mismatch repair in contingency genes.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Polymerase slippage is enhanced at short repeats and MMR efficiency drops with larger loop-outs, making these loci persistent mutational sources. A clamp-binding, repeat-targeting adaptor should kinetically bias the polymerase toward 3′→5′ editing at these sequences, reducing frameshifts at the source.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: During ESDSA in Deinococcus radiodurans, the 3′→5′ proofreading exonuclease of Pol III acts as a local anti-resection brake at invading 3′ ends, coordinating handoff to Pol I by pausing at oxidized bases; weakening this exonuclease activity will lengthen ssDNA overhangs, accelerate fragment reassembly, and increase genome misassembly.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Polymerase activities counterbalance exonucleolytic erosion during fragment reassembly, and Pol I supports BER completion that enables efficient Pol III elongation. A mechanistic way to limit erosion while sensing lesions is for Pol III’s proofreading exonuclease to backtrack at damaged bases, stabilizing the 3′ end until Pol I completes BER; reducing epsilon activity should shift this balance toward longer resection and error-prone assembly.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: MutL polymerization forms a bridge that directly biases the choice between Pol III 3′→5′ proofreading and MutH-initiated long-patch MMR: when MutL filaments reach a distant GATC, Pol III proofreading is suppressed at the mismatch to favor MutH incision; when MutL filaments are short, Pol III proofreading resolves the mismatch without MutH.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: MutL polymerizes to communicate between mismatch and distant strand discrimination sites, and MMR involves Pol III holoenzyme. This implies a checkpoint where MutL filament length regulates whether correction proceeds via local Pol III exonucleolysis versus MutH-directed excision.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: A transient downregulation of Pol III proofreading exonuclease activity is required early in ESDSA to allow synthesis past oxidized templates; after lesion encounter triggers Pol III dissociation, Pol I takes over to extend and complete BER, restoring conditions for high-fidelity Pol III elongation.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: In D. radiodurans, Pol I can elongate after Pol III dissociates at unrepaired lesions, and Pol I’s BER functions protect fragments to enable unhindered Pol III elongation. Temporarily relaxing epsilon proofreading would reduce futile cycles at damaged sites, enabling controlled polymerase switching from Pol III to Pol I and back.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: In Redβ-mediated recombineering, the fidelity of incorporating mismatched oligonucleotides is predominantly set by the 3′→5′ proofreading exonuclease of Pol III trimming the annealed 3′ ends, rather than by MMR; hypomorphic epsilon mutants will markedly increase recombineering efficiency but broaden the mutational spectrum even in MMR-proficient cells.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: MMR has little to no impact on the fidelity of the phage Red pathway, which efficiently anneals mismatched oligos. Therefore, a principal editor must be the replicative polymerase’s proofreading nuclease acting on the annealed primer termini during fill-in synthesis.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Pol III proofreading exonuclease provides kinetic proofreading that biases the MutH–Dam race toward repair by repeatedly excising and delaying ligation at nascent mismatches, thereby extending the unmethylated window and increasing the probability of MutH incision before Dam methylation.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Mismatch correction involves a race between MutH cleavage and Dam methylation, and MutH typically ‘wins’ under normal conditions. Repeated 3′→5′ excision/refix cycles by Pol III would slow sealing of the nascent strand, prolonging the period of strand discrimination and mechanistically enhancing MutH access.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: At lesion-stalled replication forks, the RecA–UmuD'2C (Pol V) activation complex directly and reversibly inhibits the 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease (ε subunit) of DNA polymerase III, suppressing polymerase idling and enabling localized TLS insertion before handoff back to replicative synthesis.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: TLS requires the absence or inhibition of the 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease, and Pol V activity is confined to RecA nucleofilaments at nonreplicable DNA. A parsimonious mechanism is that the RecA–UmuD'2C assembly allosterically dampens ε activity at stalled forks, preventing futile excision and permitting TLS insertion.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Etheno adducts (eA/eC) promote stabilized intrahelical mispairs at primer termini that reduce partitioning of the nascent 3' end to the 3'→5' exonuclease site, thereby evading proofreading and driving the observed specific misincorporations (dG opposite eA, dT opposite eC); compounds that increase primer-end fraying will restore exonucleolytic rejection and reduce adduct-induced mutagenesis.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: CAA/CEO-treated templates cause strong, specific misincorporation by E. coli Pol I. If adduct-stabilized mispairs remain intrahelical, they would be extended rather than shunted to the exonuclease site; enhancing 3' end fraying should switch the kinetic partitioning back to proofreading.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Cycles of polymerase idling at a nonreplicable template lesion generate repeatedly exposed short ssDNA at the primer terminus, which nucleates local RecA filaments and thereby constitutes the proximal spatial cue for recruiting TLS polymerases; reducing exonuclease activity diminishes this ssDNA exposure and impairs TLS efficiency.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Polymerase idling consists of successive polymerase and proofreading exonuclease turnovers at a blockage, which should transiently expose ssDNA. RecA nucleates on ssDNA and Pol V operates on RecA filaments, implying idling can seed localized SOS TLS recruitment.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Improving translation fidelity or chaperone capacity reduces spontaneous mutagenesis by preserving the metal-coordinating 3'→5' exonuclease activity of replicative polymerases from oxidative inactivation, thereby maintaining proofreading under oxidative stress conditions.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Lower translational errors reduce protein carbonylation at constant ROS and correlate with reduced mutation rates, suggesting proteome quality influences genome stability. A specific target is the proofreading exonuclease, whose activity depends on oxidation-sensitive catalytic residues; preserving it would lower replication errors.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Short tandem repeat expansions are driven by slippage that creates unpaired 3' termini; increasing the kinetic partitioning of the replicative polymerase toward its 3'→5' exonuclease site at slipped intermediates (for example, via clamp-binding peptides that destabilize the polymerase active site) will bias excision–realignment over extension and suppress repeat expansions.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Polymerase slippage in repetitive DNA confuses the replisome and promotes expansions. Since proofreading exonuclease is preferentially engaged by destabilized 3' ends, tuning polymerase–exonuclease partitioning at slippage events should mechanistically counteract expansions.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Stabilizing the pre-catalytic [DNA·dNMP·PPi] intermediate at replicative DNA polymerases with small-molecule PPi mimetics will allosterically bias the polymerase–exonuclease partition toward proofreading/rejection at mispairs and lesion-stalled 3′ ends, thereby preventing TLS polymerase engagement and reducing mutagenesis in vivo.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: PPi exchange from the [DNA·dNMP·PPi] intermediate selectively favors ‘rejection’ of incorrect dNMPs before bond formation. Pharmacologically prolonging this intermediate should increase pre-catalytic proofreading at mismatches and damage-stalled termini, maintaining idling and channeling lesions to repair rather than TLS.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Beryllium-induced carcinogenicity is mediated in part by selective inhibition of 3′→5′ proofreading exonuclease at replication forks, which converts polymerase idling at helix-distorting lesions into error-prone bypass by exonuclease-poor polymerases, enriching for dipyrimidine C→T transition signatures.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Be2+ strongly inhibits proofreading exonuclease without impairing polymerase α activity. With proofreading suppressed, lesions that normally enforce idling can be traversed by mammalian polymerases capable of copying through pyrimidine dimers, shifting the outcome from repair to mutagenic bypass.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: During D-loop extension, the ε 3′→5′ exonuclease of DNA polymerase III edits nascent heteroduplex ends by iterative excision of mismatches, acting as a recombination-proofreading module; increasing ε activity will reduce interspecies recombination even when canonical mismatch repair is disabled.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: Mismatch repair systems serve a recombination proofreading role by aborting mismatched heteroduplexes. A mechanistically analogous editing could be executed directly at the 3′ end by the Pol III exonuclease during D-loop–mediated synthesis, so tuning ε would modulate recombination fidelity independently of MMR.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: In Schizosaccharomyces pombe, proofreading exonuclease back-up at UV-stalled replisomes initiates an alternative excision pathway for CPDs/6-4PPs by generating short 3′-recessed gaps that are then recognized and incised by an ERCC1–Rad10-like endonuclease complex, functioning independently of canonical NER.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: S. pombe possesses an alternative excision route for UV photoproducts distinct from NER. A plausible trigger is the 3′→5′ exonuclease ‘backing up’ at stalled forks, creating defined recessed termini that recruit structure-specific nucleases to remove the lesion-containing oligonucleotide.

DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.hypothesis: Pharmacologic enhancement of polymerase proofreading at 5‑methylcytosine deamination hotspots will synergize with Very Short Patch Mismatch Repair (VSPMR) to suppress age-associated CpG C→T transitions by increasing pre-incision rejection of G:T mispairs before their fixation.
DNA polymerase proofreading exonuclease.rationale: VSPMR specifically repairs G:T mismatches from 5‑mC deamination, but not all lesions are corrected before replication. Increasing proofreading efficiency at G:T mispairs will decrease extension from mismatched 3′ termini, giving VSPMR more opportunity to restore G:C.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Oxidative carbonylation of MutL under ROS stress diminishes its DNA-binding/ATPase function, making MutL the rate-limiting step of MMR and transiently converting wild-type cells into a reversible mutator state without underlying MMR gene mutations.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: Protein carbonylation is identified as a dominating determinant of spontaneous mutation rates, and MutL is the limiting component when MMR is stressed. Thus, ROS-driven post-translational damage to MutL should mechanistically reduce effective MMR capacity, elevating mutation and recombination rates until proteostasis is restored.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Bacteria use stress-induced proteolysis to transiently lower MutL abundance during natural competence, selectively boosting recombination between diverged sequences while maintaining base-substitution fidelity, thereby enabling HGT-driven adaptation without a broad mutator phenotype.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: A ~4-fold reduction in MutL can uncouple recombination control from replication error correction, producing hyperrecombination without a mutator phenotype. This implies that regulated MutL downregulation could be a programmed mechanism to transiently relax the recombination barrier while minimizing deleterious point mutations.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Heterologous DNA influx during horizontal gene transfer saturates MutL on mismatch-rich recombination intermediates, depleting free MutL and increasing genome-wide fixation of replication errors; combined with SOS activation, this forms a positive feedback between recombination and mutagenesis during adaptation.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: When mismatches increase, MutL becomes limiting, saturating MMR. HGT introduces mismatch-laden heteroduplex DNA that can titrate MutL, plausibly elevating background mutation rates and synergizing with SOS mutagenesis to accelerate adaptive evolution.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Lambdoid bacteriophages encode short anti-MMR peptides that bind and sequester bacterial MutL, enabling evasion of MMR-mediated editing of phage heteroduplexes and accelerating phage genome evolution while transiently inducing a host mutator phenotype.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: Lambdoids appear to evade host editing to speed their evolution. A direct mechanism would be phage-encoded factors that target the limiting MMR hub MutL, reducing host mismatch correction on phage recombination intermediates and incidentally lowering host genomic repair fidelity.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Small-molecule allosteric activators that stabilize MutL’s mismatch-bound ATPase/clamp state will increase effective MutL stoichiometry at repair sites and prevent MMR saturation under high mismatch loads, functioning as anti-evolvability adjuvants to slow resistance emergence.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: MMR saturation arises from MutL limitation; more MutL molecules than MutS participate at a mismatch. Stabilizing active MutL complexes should raise functional capacity without overexpression, maintaining high-fidelity repair during stress and reducing adaptive mutagenesis.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: During oxidative or starvation stress, transient reduction or mistiming of Dam-directed strand discrimination converts MMR into undirected repair, rendering it mutagenic and producing short bursts of mutations comparable to MMR loss; restoration of Dam activity then returns cells to low-mutation states.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: In dam mutants, undirected MMR is as mutagenic as MMR deficiency. Stress-driven perturbations of methylation timing could mechanistically flip MMR from error-correcting to error-generating, providing a reversible, non-genetic path to a mutator phenotype during adaptation.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Front-loading therapy with high–genetic-barrier antibiotics (lacking single-step resistance routes) will selectively purge mutator subpopulations by preventing hitch-hiking of adaptive alleles and forcing lethal accrual of deleterious mutations, thereby reducing resistance emergence in subsequent treatments.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: High-dose ampicillin eliminated mutators because no simple mutational events can generate resistance, implying that when single-step escapes are unavailable mutators are disproportionately culled. Designing initial regimens around such drugs should mechanistically deplete mutators before other agents are introduced.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Immune surveillance selects for antimutator reversion or hypomorphic restoration of mismatch repair in initially MMR-deficient tumors, reducing neoantigen load and producing late-stage subclones with diminished mutational signatures despite an early mutator phenotype.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: Late selection for MMR revertants/suppressors has been proposed in tumor progression, suggesting pressure to reduce the fitness cost of a potent mutator. A plausible driver is immune pressure against hypermutated clones, favoring mechanistic restoration of MMR activity to lower antigenicity.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: RecBCD-mediated recombination is a principal engine of large adaptive gene duplications in MMR-deficient bacteria; thus, small-molecule RecBCD inhibitors will disproportionately suppress adaptive evolution and resistance acquisition in mutator populations compared to nonmutators.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: In mutL/mutS-deficient strains, duplication formation is strongly reduced by recB mutation, implicating the RecBC pathway as the mechanistic driver of this adaptive route when MMR is absent. Targeting RecBCD should therefore selectively blunt mutator-enabled duplication-based adaptation.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Combining transient inhibition of Dam methylation with administration of a base analogue that induces replication mismatches will trigger undirected MMR-dependent chromosomal degradation and selectively kill bacteria with active mismatch repair.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: In dam mutants, base-analogue treatment causes massive chromosomal loss and 10^3-fold viability reduction that depends on MutS/MutH/UvrD, indicating lethal, undirected MMR processing of mismatches on unmethylated DNA. Pharmacologically recreating this state should mechanistically convert MMR into a bactericidal liability.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Pathogens that rely on +2 frameshift–biased translational errors modulate the MnmE/GidA tRNA modification pathway under stress to raise frameshift mutation supply for antigenic variation; inhibition of MnmE/GidA will cap this frameshift-driven mutability and slow immune evasion.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: In some bacteria, predominant +2 frameshift errors are controlled by MnmE and GidA, linking tRNA modification to mutational spectra. This suggests a mechanistic lever that pathogens can tune under stress to increase phenotypic variation, and a druggable vulnerability to reduce adaptive frameshifting.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Frequent, low-intensity antibiotic dosing schedules will reduce stress-induced mutagenesis activation and thereby lower the rate of resistance emergence compared to infrequent high-intensity pulses of equal cumulative exposure.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: Stress-induced mutagenesis scales positively with selection strength and negatively with stress frequency, indicating a mechanistic dependence of mutation supply on dosing dynamics. Optimizing dosing to keep stress frequent but mild should minimize induction of mutator pathways.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Carbon-source starvation lowers intracellular S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), reducing Dam-dependent GATC methylation and impairing strand discrimination by mismatch repair; this starvation-induced hypomethylation transiently converts E. coli into a mutator/hyper-recombination state (MAC), which reverses when carbon and SAM are restored.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: MAC requires carbon-source starvation, and dam hypomethylation is known to produce mutator and hyper-recombination phenotypes. Linking starvation to reduced SAM (Dam cofactor) provides a mechanistic route for reversible MMR impairment that explains stress-dependent mutator switching.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Oxidative metabolism drives a proteome-mediated mutator switch via oxidation of the ribonucleotide pool (e.g., 8-oxo-GTP), which elevates transcriptional errors in DNA replication and mismatch repair proteins, transiently reducing MMR activity and promoting error-prone DNA synthesis during MAC.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: Oxidative damage compromises transcriptional fidelity in mutT-defective contexts, and MAC depends on oxidative metabolism. Thus, oxidized rNTPs can misencode key fidelity proteins, creating a feed-forward, reversible decrease in repair accuracy that elevates mutation rates under stress.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Stress conditions that induce MAC upregulate retron/msDNA production, and mismatched msDNA decoys sequester MutS/MutL/MutH complexes, transiently suppressing MMR to enable hypermutation and recombination; retron downregulation restores MMR and lowers mutation rates after adaptation.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: Overproduced msDNA with mismatches can sequester MMR proteins and increase mutagenesis, suggesting a physiological role for retrons as stress-inducible MMR decoys that tune mutation rates. This provides a reversible, genetically controlled mechanism for mutational ‘gear-shifting’.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: A quantitative proteome carbonylation (PC) threshold gates the SOS mutator response: below the PC threshold, oxidative proteome damage activates SOS and mutagenic polymerases while preserving viability; above the threshold, biosynthetic collapse blocks phage replication and leads to cell death.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: Phage replication in irradiated hosts declines with increasing PC even when phage DNA is intact, indicating a proteome damage threshold that impairs biosynthesis. Coupling this threshold to SOS activation explains a tunable window for stress-induced mutagenesis versus lethality.

Mutator phenotype.hypothesis: Transient, stress-induced downregulation of MMR in mutator lineages relaxes anti-recombination barriers and biases horizontal gene transfer toward uptake of intact MMR genes, producing a self-limiting oscillation between high- and low-mutation states during adaptation.
Mutator phenotype.rationale: MMR inhibits recombination across sequence-diverged genomes, while MMR loss increases recombination among mutators. A stress-regulated drop in MMR would facilitate reacquisition of antimutator alleles by recombination, mechanistically explaining evolutionary ‘gear-shifting’.

Chromosomal instability (CIN).hypothesis: Targeted re-methylation of interspersed repeats (LINEs/SINEs and segmental duplications) will suppress ectopic homologous recombination and reduce chromosomal instability in hypomethylated cancer cells by impairing homology search and strand invasion at repeat tracts.
Chromosomal instability (CIN).rationale: Cancer hypomethylation correlates with rearrangements consistent with repeat-mediated recombination; restoring methylation at repeats should mechanistically inhibit HR initiation and pairing at these sites, lowering quadriradials/translocations and LOH. This provides a precision epigenetic approach to directly dampen the major structural drivers of CIN.

Chromosomal instability (CIN).hypothesis: A protease-dependent licensing step at (peri)centromeres triggers promoter- and alkylator-induced chromosomal associations that culminate in rearrangements; inhibition of the responsible cysteine protease(s) prevents CIN without affecting point mutagenesis or SCE.
Chromosomal instability (CIN).rationale: Antipain, a protease inhibitor, selectively blocks carcinogen- and TPA-induced exchange-type aberrations and centromeric associations while leaving mutagenesis/SCE unchanged, implicating a proteolytic switch that enables recombinogenic centromere-proximal events. Identifying and inhibiting this protease should uncouple DNA damage from CIN.

Chromosomal instability (CIN).hypothesis: Engineering micro-heterology (silent base substitutions) across highly identical duplicated sequences and satellite arrays will mechanistically reduce ectopic crossover/NAHR and thereby attenuate CIN in high-risk genomes.
Chromosomal instability (CIN).rationale: More diverged repeats are more stable against ectopic recombination, and repeated sequences drive rearrangements; strategically increasing benign divergence within repeat tracts should impair D-loop formation and Holliday junction stabilization between ectopic sites, reducing translocations and deletions.

Chromosomal instability (CIN).hypothesis: Cancer hypomethylation initiates a positive feedback loop wherein increased repeat-mediated gene conversion homogenizes dispersed repeats, raising sequence identity and further amplifying ectopic recombination and CIN; early targeted remethylation breaks this loop and stabilizes the genome.
Chromosomal instability (CIN).rationale: If repeats were identical, ectopic HR would scramble the genome; hypomethylation allows such recombination, which then homogenizes repeats, making future events more likely. Intervening at the methylation step should mechanistically halt repeat homogenization and subsequent CIN propagation.

Chromosomal instability (CIN).hypothesis: For DNA damage that seeds recombination intermediates, forcing DNA-synthesis-independent chromatin assembly immediately after break formation will bias repair toward noncrossover pathways and reduce chromosome rearrangements.
Chromosomal instability (CIN).rationale: Two chromatin assembly routes exist; rapid nucleosome assembly independent of DNA synthesis should occlude branch migration/resolvase access and favor dissolution over resolution of Holliday junctions, lowering reciprocal crossovers and translocations that drive CIN.

Chromosomal instability (CIN).hypothesis: Small molecules that stabilize mismatched Holliday junctions will promote RTR (BLM–TOP3A–RMI)-mediated dissolution over endonucleolytic resolution, thereby suppressing crossover-driven CIN in mismatch-repair–deficient cells.
Chromosomal instability (CIN).rationale: Highly mismatched Holliday junctions are relatively stable, and MMR-deficient cells fail to dismantle mismatched recombination intermediates, leading to CIN; pharmacologically stabilizing these junctions should extend the window for dissolution and reduce crossovers and translocations.

Transposable elements.hypothesis: Dps-driven toroidal DNA condensation creates a diffusion-limited ‘physical checkpoint’ that globally suppresses transposition rates while biasing insertion events toward transcriptionally open loci that escape condensation, thereby reshaping target-site selection of transposable elements during stationary phase.
Transposable elements.rationale: DNA toroids restrict molecular diffusion, forming a molecular cage that should slow the target search of transposases and reduce access to compacted chromatin. In stationary phase, when TE activity can rise, such physical compaction would selectively permit insertions where DNA remains accessible, shifting the transposition landscape without changing transposase abundance.

Transposable elements.hypothesis: Dynamic switching between long-patch and very-short-patch mismatch repair (LPMR/VSPMR) cooperates with cytosine methylation to inactivate transposable elements by preferentially introducing and fixing transitions at their termini, accelerating end-divergence that disrupts transposase recognition while sparing internal sequences for potential domestication.
Transposable elements.rationale: Eukaryotic genomes likely require both LPMR and VSPMR; methylation-driven silencing and RIP/MIP-like processes are implicated in TE inactivation. A mechanistic synergy in which MMR subpathways, biased toward transition mispair processing at methylated TE boundaries, would drive rapid divergence of TE ends and selectively cripple mobility.

Transposable elements.hypothesis: Precise excision of DNA transposons is promoted by transient R-loops forming at terminal inverted repeats that enable copy-choice recombination, and helicase II (MutU/UvrD) suppresses this pathway by resolving these RNA–DNA hybrids; targeted R-loop stabilization at TE ends can therefore program precise excision.
Transposable elements.rationale: Helicase II strongly prevents precise excision in a system consistent with copy-choice mechanisms, suggesting a nucleic-acid structure that UvrD resolves. R-loops at repetitive termini would stabilize template switching during excision, predicting that engineered R-loop formation at TE ends promotes precise, footprint-free removal.

Transposable elements.hypothesis: In Deinococcus radiodurans lacking RecA, restricted diffusion within toroidally condensed nucleoids elevates local concentrations of identical insertion sequences, enabling IS-encoded recombinases to catalyze inter-replicon fusions; modulating nucleoid condensation should thus steer IS-mediated genome remodeling across its multiple circular elements.
Transposable elements.rationale: IS elements mediate specific genome rearrangements in D. radiodurans recA mutants. Toroidal DNA caging restricts diffusion and raises effective local homology, which would favor IS–IS synapsis and recombination across different circular replicons, providing a physical lever to direct large-scale architecture changes.

Transposable elements.hypothesis: Conserved insertion sequences act as MEPS-satisfying ‘identity anchors’ that nucleate RecA-mediated D-loops and overcome homeologous barriers during conjugation, enabling large-fragment horizontal gene transfer across species; conversely, accelerated diversification of IS sequences establishes a TE-centered speciation barrier.
Transposable elements.rationale: Insertion sequences function as dispersed homology blocks capable of mediating rearrangements. If these blocks meet minimal homology requirements, they can seed recombination and drag flanking DNA across divergent genomes during conjugation, explaining observed large-fragment cross-species integrations and predicting that IS diversification throttles such transfers.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: In E. coli, local GATC site density creates sinks for MutL via stable MutH–GATC complexes, transiently sequestering MutL and throttling mismatch repair throughput elsewhere; housekeeping genes have evolved reduced local GATC density to prioritize their own repair and minimize mutation accumulation.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: MutL appears functionally limiting despite equimolar MutS, implying post-translational sequestration rather than abundance differences. Because MutH forms stable complexes at GATC sites, regions rich in GATC could titrate MutL, leaving fewer free molecules for active repair at other loci. Selection would favor lowered GATC density near essential housekeeping genes to ensure preferential access to MMR and maintain their fidelity.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: Oxidative carbonylation of conserved residues in MutL-family proteins acts as a molecular switch that impairs MutS–MutL complex formation and endonuclease activity, shifting cells toward SOS/TLS-dependent mutagenesis; tissues or organisms with lower proteome carbonylation maintain higher MMR capacity and accumulate fewer age-related mutations.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: Protein activity decreases with increasing carbonylation, and oxidative protein damage rises with age. If carbonylation targets functional domains in MutL, it would reduce MMR efficiency and tilt the balance toward error-prone lesion bypass under stress, mechanistically explaining age-associated mutator phenotypes.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: Pol IV (DinB) performs a housekeeping function by resolving transcription–replication conflicts through beta-clamp–mediated gap filling at RNA–DNA hybrid-associated stalls independently of canonical SOS induction, which explains the housekeeping-like selective constraints observed at dinB and why its loss elevates basal SOS signaling and genome instability even without exogenous damage.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: dinB exhibits selective constraints akin to housekeeping genes despite not being highly expressed, implying an essential basal role. A conflict-resolution mechanism that prevents fork collapse and SOS activation would reconcile these evolutionary signatures with cellular physiology.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: Engineering cells for higher translational fidelity dampens endogenous activation of mutagenic damage tolerance pathways (dinB/umuDC in bacteria and RAD30 in yeast) by alleviating proteotoxic and oxidative stress, thereby lowering genome-wide mutation rates and improving long-term genetic stability of biotechnology strains.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: Reducing translation errors improves proteome quality and functional activity per protein, lowering proteostasis burden. Because stress-responsive mutator systems activate under proteotoxic/oxidative stress, raising fidelity should mechanistically reduce their induction and the mutation load.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: In mammalian housekeeping genes, CpG-depleted intronic tracts of roughly 120–570 nt are preferentially methylated and recruit methylation-dependent recombination suppressors, forming local recombination cold spots that protect essential coding regions and enhance chromosomal stability in gene-dense housekeeping clusters.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: DNA methylation can suppress homologous recombination, and CpG island length constraints suggest defined tract sizes for regulatory modules. Positioning recombination-suppressive, methylation-prone segments within housekeeping gene introns provides a mechanism to preserve exon integrity and maintain stable expression.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: Housekeeping genes have evolved codon usage and local sequence contexts that minimize the functional impact of transcriptional 8‑oxo‑GTP–induced errors and GA-repeat–driven frameshifts, by depleting error-prone motifs and enriching error-buffering synonymous codons, thereby preserving essential proteome function under oxidative stress.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: Oxidized NTPs (8-oxo-GTP) drive specific transcription errors, and GA repeats promote frameshifting; fidelity factors like MutT and tRNA modification systems constrain these errors. Selection should shape essential (housekeeping) coding sequences to be intrinsically robust to these predictable error modes.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: During stationary-phase and stress, σS-driven transcriptional reprogramming reorganizes the nucleoid so that essential housekeeping loci are embedded in highly transcribed, transcription-coupled repair (TCR)-enriched domains, biasing repair toward these regions when MMR is downregulated and SOS/TLS activity rises, thereby diverting mutagenesis to nonessential loci.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: Stress downregulates MMR while inducing σS and elevating mutagenic polymerases; transcription machinery broadly participates in NER/TCR. A mechanistic triage via nucleoid architecture would protect housekeeping genes while allowing adaptive mutagenesis elsewhere.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: The Dam/Dcm methylation landscape is non-randomly arranged around housekeeping genes to enhance MutHLS strand discrimination and to provide Dcm-dependent very-short-patch repair as a backup when MMR saturates, thereby preferentially safeguarding essential loci under high replication or stress loads.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: MMR can saturate and relies on methylation for strand discrimination; Dcm-dependent VSP repair specifically corrects T:G mismatches at 5mC sites. A patterned methylation architecture around essential genes would mechanistically prioritize their repair.

Housekeeping genes.hypothesis: Low-complexity hydrophilic regions appended to housekeeping proteins in desiccation/irradiation‑resistant bacteria act as metabolite/metal-binding scaffolds that locally concentrate Mn2+–phosphate–amino acid radioprotective complexes, creating microenvironments that prevent protein carbonylation and sustain essential enzymatic activities under ROS stress.
Housekeeping genes.rationale: Proteome protection in D. radiodurans depends on low–molecular weight Mn2+–metabolite complexes, and many DNA/protein fate proteins carry hydrophilic LC regions linked to desiccation tolerance. LC regions can bind metabolites/metals and may scaffold protective complexes around essential enzymes.
